grammar.title: 6B: Modals of deduction - might, can't, must
grammar.explanation:
We use **might**, **can't**, and **must** to guess about now. They help us say what we think is true.

Use **must** when you are almost sure. The library **must** be open. I see many people inside.

Use **can't** when you are almost sure it is NOT true. She **can't** be at the museum. It is closed today.

Use **might** when you are not sure. The restaurant **might** be full. It is Saturday night.

After **might**, **can't**, and **must**, use the verb without to. He works at the pharmacy, so he **must be** tired.
examples: *The library *must* be open.* (I see many people inside)
*She *can't* be at the museum.* (it is closed today)
*The restaurant *might* be full.* (it is Saturday night)
*He *must* be tired.* (he works at the pharmacy all day)
*The cafe *might* be closed.* (I do not see the lights)

practice.q: Complete with might, can't, or must: 'It ___ be ten o'clock. I see the pharmacy is open.'
practice.a: must (I am almost sure it is open)

practice.q: Which word means 'I am not sure'?
Is this sentence correct: 'She must to be at home'?
practice.a: No. After must we use the verb without 'to': 'She must be at home.'
